text: 2026: The Year AI Film Went Long-Form The state of the field as of October 2026. This chapter is a dated snapshot, not doctrine: model versions, prices, and festival rules move fast. Every claim below carries its source; single-sourced items are flagged. For the machine-readable model data, see api/v1/models.json per-model last verified , status , what changed , sources . The headline: a fully AI-generated feature premiered at a major festival On June 10, 2026, Tribeca premiered Dreams of Violets — a 75-minute docudrama by Fountain 0 written/directed/produced by Ash Koosha, co-produced by Pooya Koosha . Fountain 0 describes it as the first feature-length live-action film completely generated by AI to be accepted to a major festival. The film is a fictionalized dramatization of the January 2026 Iranian protests: five strangers hiding in a dead-end Tehran alley at dawn, a violent soldier who discovers them, and Amir — a 10-year-old boy with cerebral palsy — watching from a window and deciding to act. Every image and person in it was AI-generated; the story was built from journalistic reports, photographs, and eyewitness accounts. The documented production stack businesswire.com and consequence.net, May 27, 2026 : - Video generation: Kling AI - Language editing: Anthropic Claude - Research and imagery: Google Gemini + Nano Banana - Blocking and frame accuracy: Fountain 0's own technology The headline numbers: made in three months for ~$2,000 Fountain 0 executive chairman Tom Rogers cited "incredibly efficient cost management techniques" . Tribeca co-founder Jane Rosenthal endorsed the selection on the strength of "the emotional immediacy and urgency of the story itself." Ash Koosha addressed the ethics directly: a film about people who actually died "raises difficult questions," he said — his answer was that silence and forgetting were worse, and "the dead deserve to be witnessed." The film later became rentable on Fountain 0's own site Wikipedia, Dreams of Violets . What this actually proves: a feature can now be produced for the price of a used laptop — but the film was still human-directed end to end written, directed, produced by the Koosha brothers, with a language-editing pass . It is a production-cost revolution, not an authorship one. A shot-by-shot teardown of its documented craft is in api/v1/teardowns.json "Dreams of Violets" . The 2026 model field: 4K + native audio is the baseline By October 2026 the field had consolidated around 4K output and native audio as table stakes. title: Higgsfield Platform Mastery
headings: The model roster (what to use when)
text: Higgsfield Platform Mastery The model roster what to use when Higgsfield is model-agnostic — it hosts many engines under one credit pool. Third-party model guides rank them this way tiers: Free / Low 0.1–2 credits / Mid 2–10 / Premium 10+ : Need Model Tier --- --- --- Top-tier cinematic video + native audio Kling 3.0 Premium Epic scale / spectacle Kling 3.0 Premium Nature / landscapes + reference images Veo 3.1 Premium Artistic / stylized video Wan 2.6 Mid Fast iteration Seedance 2.0 Pro Mid VFX / fluid motion Minimax Hailuo 2.3 Mid Budget-friendly video Kling 2.5 Turbo / Higgsfield DoP Lite Free–Low Image side: Soul 2.0 fashion/aesthetic, free , Soul Cinema cinematic stills with film grain and era-aware styling , Nano Banana Pro photorealistic, low cost , Soul Cast AI actor generation . Key insight: a clip made through Higgsfield on the Kling engine is a Kling clip — what differs is how you buy it shared credit pool and what you can steer presets vs raw prompt control . Going to Kling directly exposes controls Higgsfield's preset UI hides: end-frame pinning, multi-reference elements , multi-prompt shots, 3–15s durations. Cinema Studio — the filmmaking layer Cinema Studio is Higgsfield's director-mode workspace: - Camera movement controls: static, handheld, zoom, pan, dolly, orbit and more — several moves can be stacked in one shot - Genre settings: Action, Epic, Drama, Comedy, Horror — the whole scene follows the genre's look and pacing - Era selection: regrade to look like the 1960s, 1980s, 1990s, or today - AI Cast: build custom AI actors with chosen look, outfit, era, personality - Scene building: place locations and props, shape the frame - Emotions: choose what each character shows - Color grading: fine-tune color, temperature, contrast, presets - Multiple references: upload many reference images to guide generation - Real-time co-directing: invite teammates onto one project - AI assistant: help with camera angles, lighting, prompts, script-to-shot breakdowns It isn't tied to one model — pick the best engine per shot. Generation controls that matter - Start frame: upload or generate the opening image; the clip grows from it. This is the single biggest quality lever. - End frame where supported : pin exactly where a camera move finishes — turns drift into intention. - Camera movement presets: faster than prompt engineering; pick the move, don't describe it. - Duration: longer clips cost more and drift more. Short, locked shots chain better than long wandering ones. - Aspect ratio: match your delivery format from the first generation, never crop later. Turbo vs Standard thinking - Standard / Premium models Kling 3.0 etc. : hero shots — faces, dialogue, key story beats. - Turbo / Lite models: iteration, B-roll, establishers, tests. Draft cheap, render the winners expensive. - One clip at a time, quality-gated: a failed clip never chains. Re-prompt, don't hope. Reliability rules 1. Never spend credits on a guess — pre-check the prompt against the checklists in prompt-engineering.md . 2. Failed/NSFW generations aren't billed on the API path; verify billing behavior in the app before a big batch. 3. Credits reset each billing cycle and don't roll over — plan usage so paid credits don't evaporate. 4. Higgsfield open-sourced three of its own AI films with every prompt, camera setting, and asset published — mine those before inventing your own pipeline. title: Higgsfield Prompt Engineering
headings: The anatomy of a prompt that works
Camera phrasing that the models obey
text: Higgsfield Prompt Engineering The anatomy of a prompt that works Treat the prompt as a directing system, not a description. Every generation should specify, in order: 1. Subject — who/what, locked identity 2. Micro-action — one believable action, not three 3. Environment — where, with subtle motion in it 4. Camera behavior — one intentional move see below 5. Lighting design — explicit and physical "golden-hour side light, long shadows" 6. Visual style — cinematic, anamorphic, film grain, era 7. Emotional tone — the feeling of the shot 8. Physics & motion details — how things move cloth in breeze, steam rising 9. Rendering quality modifiers — 4K, shallow depth of field, stable architecture Missing layers = randomness. "Slow dolly push-in" beats "zoom in." Explicit lighting beats "nice lighting." Camera phrasing that the models obey - Push-in / reveal: "the camera slowly dollies toward the subject with smooth stabilized movement" - Pull-back / scale: "the camera slowly pulls backward, gradually revealing the enormous environment surrounding the subject" - Orbit: "camera orbits 360° around the subject" - Pan: "slow camera pan across the scene" - Stacked moves: Higgsfield's Cinema Studio supports several moves in one shot — but one motivated move beats two unmotivated ones. Rule: every movement needs a purpose. Ask what the move reveals or withholds. The Soul ID prompting rule When a Soul ID character is active, do not re-describe the face or core features — the Soul ID handles that. Describe only what changes: wardrobe, setting, action, expression, camera, light, style. Good: "The Soul ID character now wears a formal black suit, standing at a podium addressing a conference room. Camera: dolly in toward her face. Style: cinematic, cool corporate lighting." The exclusion block Always exclude what breaks cinematic output: morphing faces, extra limbs, melting hands, warping architecture, flicker, watermark-like artifacts, text in frame unless wanted . Put it in every prompt, not just the risky ones. Per-shot discipline - One shot = one fully self-contained prompt. Restate the full premise every time — the model has no memory of your last clip. - Don't ask for too many actions in five seconds. One action per clip. - Keep the frame uncrowded. Fewer subjects = fewer failure modes. - Image-to-video start frame first beats text-to-video for control. Generate the still, approve it, then animate. Common failure modes and fixes Failure Fix --- --- Face morphs mid-shot Shorter clip; Soul ID or reference image; re-generate from a locked start frame Melting hands Keep hands out of frame or still; exclude "deformed hands"; crop in post Camera drift unmotivated Pin an end frame; name one explicit camera move; shorten duration Identity drift across shots Soul ID; same seed discipline; approved-frame library as start frames Flicker / texture boil Regenerate; avoid overly busy backgrounds; stabilize in post Plasticky faces in wide shots Shoot closer; composite a close-shot face in post Sources - https://higgsfield.ai/creator-hub/help-center/ai-models/how-do-i-create-and-use-a-soul-id-character - https://github.com/ianfr13/higgsfield-ai-prompt-skill/blob/HEAD/mnt/user-data/outputs/higgsfield/skills/higgsfield-soul/SKILL.md - https://github.com/servanter/ai-magic/blob/HEAD/content/blog/best-ai-video-generators-2026-sora-runway-kling-pika-comparison.mdx - https://medium.com/@gencaycubuk/i-tested-dozens-of-runway-prompts-this-framework-creates-cinematic-ai-videos-every-time-e171658033e1 - http://answerbeam.blogspot.com/2026/10/how-to-generate-video-from-image-with.html

title: Soul ID Deep Dive
headings: When to use it / when to skip it
text: Soul ID Deep Dive What it is Soul ID is Higgsfield's character-consistency layer: train it once on photos of one person and the same face appears across every generation — any style, pose, lighting, or angle. It's the equivalent of casting the same actor for the entire film. A reference image anchors a single generation but drifts across many. Soul ID trains a reusable identity once and holds it. How to train official requirements From Higgsfield's help center: 1. Open higgsfield.ai → Soul → Train new character 2. Prepare photos: 20 or more of the same person up to 80 supported - High-quality and well-lit - Face from different angles and expressions - No sunglasses, no heavy shadows, no cropped faces - Include at least one full-height photo - Recent photos for the most accurate likeness - Only your own face or someone who gave permission 3. Upload and start training — takes a few minutes 4. Name the character 5. Generate — select it in the Character tab Using it in production - Soul ID locks identity; everything else follows your prompt. Wardrobe, setting, action, camera, light — all prompt-driven. - Prompting rule: never re-describe the face. Describe only what changes from the base character. - Works across the Soul family Soul 2.0, Soul Cinema, Cinema Studio, Marketing Studio, supported video models . - Caveat: Soul IDs are tied to the model they were trained in — a character trained in Soul 2.0 may need retraining for Soul Cinema. Verify before a big shoot. When to use it / when to skip it Use: multi-shot sequences, short films with a recurring protagonist, series content, AI influencers, brand mascots, action sequences needing the same hero. Skip: single one-off shots overkill , or when you want maximum creative variation — consistency limits style range. Identity drift: causes and fixes - Drift across many generations: re-anchor with the trained Soul ID selected; don't fall back to per-generation reference uploads. - Wide-shot face collapse: faces go plasticky at distance — shoot closer, or composite a close-shot face in post. - Feature drift: keep a character sheet front, 3/4, side reference and use it as the reference image when drift appears. - Never fabricate identity frames. The trained Soul ID is the identity authority — every clip's face must trace back to it, never to an invented start frame. title: Competition-entry craft
headings: The constraint set that shapes production
text: Competition-entry craft Judged AI-film competitions are a production teacher, not a lottery ticket. This chapter is about what their constraints and judging criteria teach you about making professional work — whether or not you ever enter one. Why competitions are worth studying A competition hands you three things most productions never get: 1. Hard constraints — runtime limits, delivery specs, content rules. Constraints are a forcing function for craft: every decision the rules make for you is a decision you can't get wrong. 2. A published quality bar — judging criteria tell you exactly what experienced eyes score: directing, craft, sound, originality. That's a checklist you can aim any film at. 3. A body of judged work — winning entries are public. Shot-by-shot teardowns of what placed are the cheapest film school available see case-studies/competition-teardowns.md . The constraint set that shapes production Real competition rulebooks converge on the same production discipline. Treat each as a standing habit: - Runtime discipline. Competitions cap entries at a few minutes. The craft lesson: a 3-minute film that lands beats a 10-minute film that drifts. Budget your runtime like your credits — every shot must earn its seconds. - Delivery specs are real. Watermarks, packshots, aspect ratios, masters. The craft lesson: professional delivery is a package, not a file. Build your delivery checklist before you lock picture see skills/delivery/ . - Rights hygiene. Competition rules typically require AI-generated music/voice/sound with rights held by the creator. The craft lesson: clear every asset's rights at generation time, not at delivery. Keep the receipts in your asset registry. - Likeness safety. "No real person's face or voice" is a common rule — not even your own. The craft lesson: never build a film on likeness you can't clear. Synthetic characters and Soul IDs are the safe default. - Small teams, async. Winning entries are routinely made by 2–4 people across time zones. The craft lesson: a tight team with a shared asset registry beats a large team with a group chat. What juries actually reward Across Runway AIFF, Project Odyssey, Reply AIFF, the Higgsfield Action Contest, and MIT's hackathon, judges reward the same things: story over spectacle, authorial intent, character/POV discipline, originality, sound design, and polish as the floor. They punish: visible morphing/inconsistency, generic "AI slop," tech demos without narrative, and AI that pulls focus from the story. Distilled: narrative cohesion + committed POV + intentional AI use + pro-grade sound + consistent visuals. Originality is the tiebreaker; polish is the entry ticket. Direct for that jury — story, cinematography, craft — not for the AI-tools audience. The film that wins is the one that would work if nobody knew how it was made. Craft patterns from judged work Higgsfield's Action Contest 8,752 submissions, 139 countries shows what experienced filmmakers do with AI: - "GRANDMA vs WASP" — Muhannad Nassar & Simon Meyer. The makers never met in person; fully async workflow across time zones. Lesson: decentralized production works when the asset pipeline is disciplined. - "CUPID" — Shestak Nikolay, actor/filmmaker. Concepts that would need prohibitive traditional budgets. Lesson: AI used for impossible scale, not novelty. - "SCRATCH" — Ash & Aram Gevorkyan, made in five days . Director + 3D/VFX generalist duo; production value audiences mistook for a studio trailer. Lesson: a tight team with real craft compresses schedules AI can't compress alone. Pattern: experienced filmmakers using AI for impossible scale, tight teams, real craft — not tech demos. Study the open-sourced winners Higgsfield open-sourced three of its own AI films with every prompt, camera setting, and asset published. title: Story Structure for AI Short Films
headings: Story Structure for AI Short Films
text: Story Structure for AI Short Films The short-film engine A 3–5 minute AI film needs exactly three things: 1. One want — the protagonist wants something concrete, visible on screen 2. One obstacle — something specific stands in the way 3. One turn — the moment everything changes Most AI-film losers are tech demos with no second act: pretty shots, no turn. Judges especially Oscar-caliber ones punish this first. The judged-short template - Cold open 0:00–0:30 : drop into the world mid-action. No setup, no title cards explaining the premise. - Escalation 0:30–2:30 : the want meets the obstacle, pressure builds. Each shot raises the stakes or deepens the world. - Reversal 2:30–3:30 : the turn — the plan fails, the truth lands, the choice gets made. - Button 3:30–5:00 : one final image that reframes everything before it. End on the image, not on explanation. Writing for the model Design scenes around what AI renders well; write away from what it doesn't. Lean into: single subjects, strong silhouettes, weather and atmosphere, landscapes, slow deliberate motion, objects and environments, stylized looks. Write around: complex hand action, crowd choreography, intricate dialogue scenes, fast fight choreography, text/signage in frame, real people or voices festival rules forbid them anyway . The constraint is the style: the best AI films don't hide the medium — they pick stories the medium tells better than live action could impossible scale, dream logic, metamorphosis . Scene design checklist per scene - One clear want visible in the frame - One action per shot, five seconds or less each - The turn is a visual event, not dialogue - Every scene either raises stakes or deepens world — never both vaguely, never neither - The ending image is planned before the first shot is generated

title: Cinematic Language
headings: Shot sizes — what each one is for
Lighting — write it like a gaffer
text: Cinematic Language The shot vocabulary and camera grammar that make AI video read as cinema instead of a screensaver. Shot sizes — what each one is for Shot Use --- --- Extreme wide World, scale, isolation Wide Geography — where the story happens Medium Action and dialogue — the workhorse Close-up Emotion, decision, detail Extreme close-up Texture, eyes, objects that matter Festival rule of thumb: earn your close-ups. Wide → medium → close builds pressure; starting close spends it. Camera movements — the working lexicon Move Prompt phrasing Good for --- --- --- Dolly in / push-in "camera slowly dollies toward the subject, smooth stabilized movement" Portraits, reveals, rising tension Dolly out / pull-back "camera pulls backward, revealing the environment around the subject" Scale, aftermath, loneliness Pan "slow camera pan across the scene" Surveys, transitions between subjects Orbit "camera orbits around the subject" Hero moments, product, dance Crane "camera rises and pulls back, revealing the scene from above" Endings, scope Handheld "subtle handheld shake, documentary feel" Urgency, realism — use sparingly Static "locked-off static camera" Dialogue, tension, confidence "Slow dolly push-in" beats "zoom in" every time — name the physical move, not the effect. Motivated vs unmotivated: every move must reveal or withhold something. A drifting camera with no purpose is the 1 tell of amateur AI video. If you can't say why the camera moves, lock it off. Lighting — write it like a gaffer Vague lighting gets vague images. Specify direction, quality, and color: - Direction: side light, backlight/rim, top light, underlight - Quality: hard noon sun, soft overcast, flickering torchlight, neon spill - Color/temperature: golden-hour warmth, cold blue night, sodium-orange street - Motivation: every light needs a source in the world — window, lamp, neon sign Example: "dramatic golden-hour side lighting with long shadows" will always beat "nice lighting." Composition - Rule of thirds: place the subject off-center; give the frame somewhere to breathe - Depth staging: foreground, midground, background all doing something — this is what makes AI shots feel expensive - Leading lines: roads, corridors, light beams pulling the eye to the subject - Negative space: emptiness is a compositional choice — isolation, scale, dread - Don't overcrowd: fewer subjects per frame = fewer failure modes The "cinematic" recipe "Cinematic" is not a word you add — it's five things combined: 1. Camera — one intentional movement 2. Subject — one believable action 3. Environment — subtle motion dust, smoke, cloth, water 4. Lighting — explicit, motivated, consistent 5. Texture — film grain, anamorphic cues, shallow depth of field Example: "Slow cinematic dolly forward toward an ancient temple entrance. Priests walk calmly up stone steps while torch flames flicker. Thin smoke rises into warm evening air. Cloth banners move gently in the breeze. Stable architecture, realistic human motion, dramatic golden-hour lighting." Note: every movement has a purpose, and the prompt asks for exactly one action per subject. title: Character Consistency
text: Character Consistency The technical discipline of keeping people and worlds stable across shots. This is where most festival entries die. The identity stack ranked by reliability 1. Trained identity Soul ID : the gold standard. Train once on 20–80 photos; the face holds across every generation. See higgsfield/soul-id-deep-dive.md . 2. Character sheet as reference: front / 3/4 / side views of the character, used as the reference image whenever drift appears. 3. Per-generation reference upload: anchors one generation; drifts across many. Fine for single shots, not films. 4. Text description alone: weakest. Never rely on prose to hold a face across 50 shots. A documented build. Robert Gaudette's "A Face Only a Mother Could Love" — the 8-minute solo short that took the $50K Runway AIFF 2026 Grand Prix and the Reply AI Film Festival 2026 prize — was built character-sheets-first: he generated initial AI character sheets for the cast before any shots, and credits them for holding the characters' distinctive physicality coherent across the film his own account; the tool identity is reported, not audited — the Reply press release names Grok, Nano Banana, and Seedance; his escape.ai page tags Dreamina and Gemini AI . Marcel's facial disfigurement is exactly the trait that drifts shot-to-shot without a locked reference — the sheet made the trait lockable. See the full shot-by-shot teardown teardown.html ../teardown.html — "The Character Sheets Came First" . A second documented build. Tim Simmons' Dragon Blue ran the same idea through an agent: his "production office" pipeline generates Character Reference Grids and 2×2 Scene Grids as stage one, and video generation only ever executes locked stills — composition decisions happen at image cost, not video cost. The grids are curated from a "spray and select" run on Luma's Agent Board, and the Nano Banana Pro stills were chosen over Nano Banana 2 for cinematic framing his own published account . See the full shot-by-shot teardown "The Production Office" and the new agentic production office agentic-production-office.html chapter for the file contract that runs it. Wardrobe and props lock - Write the wardrobe once, in exact language, and paste it verbatim into every prompt: "worn brown leather jacket, white t-shirt, dark jeans, scuffed boots." - Props get the same treatment: one description, reused exactly. - If the wardrobe changes mid-film it should, for story , that's a new locked description — never improvise it per shot. World consistency - Locations: generate and approve a master still of each location first. Every shot in that location starts from it or references it. - Lighting continuity: lock time of day and light direction per scene. "Golden-hour side light from frame left" in every prompt of the scene. - Era/grade: pick the era and color palette up front Higgsfield's era selection helps ; don't grade shot-by-shot and hope. The chaining discipline - Last-frame chaining: every clip starts from the last frame of the previous approved clip. Never fabricate a start frame. - Approved-frame library: keep every approved still/frame. New shots start from library frames, not fresh generations. - Rejection rules: a clip fails if the face drifts, wardrobe changes, the light flips, or the camera moves without motivation. Failed clips don't chain — they get re-prompted. - One human per start frame for character-led work : crowded frames multiply failure modes. The consistency checklist before any generation - Identity system chosen and trained Soul ID for films - Wardrobe description locked, verbatim - Location master stills approved - Light direction + time of day locked per scene - Start frame is real approved frame or trained identity , never invented

title: Directing Performance in AI Video
headings: Take workflows: rehearsal as a department
text: Directing Performance in AI Video AI models don't act. They render plausible arrangements of pixels that read as acting when the direction is specific enough — and collapse into mannequin theater when it isn't. This chapter is the directing discipline behind believable AI performance, drawn from productions that solved it in public. The core problem Passport Rush's team documented it openly: AI struggles with subtle character acting. The failure has a shape: - Faces average toward neutral — micro-expressions collapse into a pleasant blank - Emotion labels "she looks devastated" produce stock expressions, not felt ones - Dead, glassy eyes — the single fastest tell of an undirected AI performance - The Verge's review of Cully Hill Boys noted "occasionally weak character interactions" as a visible limit even at $2M The fix is not a better model. It's direction written the way actors need it — as tasks , not adjectives. Direct, don't describe ONEIRIC's acting skill tig-acting-task replaced emotion labels with acting tasks entirely. The closing rule of that production: direct, don't describe — scene event, motive, goal, obstacle, tactic. Instead of description Write direction --- --- She looks devastated She is trying not to cry in front of him — jaw set, eyes on the door He is furious He is deciding whether to hit him — weight shifting forward, hands opening and closing They are in love She keeps finding reasons to stand closer; he keeps noticing and not moving away He is nervous He is rehearsing what to say — lips moving silently, thumb rubbing the ring Every entry on the right is a playable tactic — something a body can do. Models can't render "devastated." They can render a jaw set and eyes fixed on a door. Give the eyes a job The single highest-leverage performance note in the research: "dead, glassy eyes are never fixed with lighting — they're fixed by giving the eyes a job." The CINEDANCE prompt architecture gives GAZE/EYELINES its own block before blocking. In practice: - Name the eyeline target per beat: Mara holds on Vex's hands until "the ledger" — then snaps to his eyes - Eyes move between targets; they never "look sad into the middle distance" - Avert, hold, search, track — eye verbs are direction, not decoration - In dialogue coverage, the listener's eyes do half the acting — cut to the listener If a performance feels dead, check the eyes first. Nine times out of ten there's no eyeline written. One feeling per shot AI can't play an arc inside a single clip. It can hold one tactic for 4–8 seconds. So: - Break emotional turns into separate shots — the turn happens in the cut - The reaction shot is your best friend: AI renders listening better than it renders complex feeling - Moment-to-moment tactics tied to dialogue words the tig-acting-task block form : each line gets its own tactic, each tactic its own shot if needed The director's read Before generating a scene, ONEIRIC's pipeline produced a "director's read": the one shared event every character lives through, plus each character's physical channel for it. Everyone in the scene is experiencing the same event — but grief lives in Mara's hands, in Vex's jaw, in the kid's feet. Write the event once, then assign each character their channel. This is what keeps ensemble scenes from becoming four mannequins emoting at the camera. Casting the face Consistent identity reads as good acting. A face that drifts 5% between shots reads as a bad performance even when the "acting" is fine: - Lock the face anchor; never re-run the base portrait - State changes dirt, wounds, tears are masked integrations, not re-generations - For recurring characters, identity systems Soul ID and equivalents beat per-prompt description The audience forgives a limited performance from a consistent face. It never forgives a great "take" from a stranger. Ration the close-up Micro-acting is the weakest link in every current model. Spend close-ups at emotional peaks — that's where the audience looks ha

title: Color Grading AI Footage
text: Color Grading AI Footage Every AI generation arrives with its own built-in grade — the model's idea of what "cinematic" looks like, baked into the pixels. On a multi-shot production, that's 40 different colorists who never met. The colorist's job on AI footage is unification : bringing neighboring shots to one look. The two places color lives In the plate before generation . Lens character, palette direction, texture, time-of-day — baked into the location/character image plates. What you bake, you don't have to fix. The ONEIRIC rule: the plate itself becomes the lens. In the grade after generation . Shot-to-shot matching, the show look, technical delivery. What the plate couldn't hold. Decide per element which place it lives. Anything the video model keeps dropping belongs in the plate. Anything that needs to move across the whole film belongs in the grade. The unification pass Before any creative grading, unify. Pick one hero shot per scene as the reference. For every other shot: 1. Match exposure and white balance to the reference scopes, not eyes 2. Match contrast curve — AI generations vary wildly in black level 3. Match saturation — see the de-plasticize stack below 4. Only then apply the creative look Do the unification pass over the location set before generating where possible the ADILIADA production did this — it's cheaper than discovering mismatch in the grade. The de-plasticize stack AI footage has a recognizable syndrome: over-smooth gradients, over-saturated color, waxy skin, a sheen over everything. The fix, in order: 1. Desaturate 10–20%. AI oversaturates by default. This one move does half the work. 2. Add fine film grain. 35mm grain breaks up the smooth gradients that scream synthetic. Grain is the fastest anti-plastic pass in existence. 3. Subtle chromatic aberration at high-contrast edges. Real lenses have flaws; perfect edges read as rendered. 4. Soften, don't sharpen. Plastic + sharp = worse. A whisper of diffusion beats any sharpening pass. 5. Skin last. Skin is the hardest surface — if it's waxy, a dedicated skin-refinement pass or slight diffusion on skin tones only. Check the whole stack on a big screen. Defects invisible on a laptop appear at 4K. Matching across models Different models have different "house grades" — Kling's contrast curve isn't Veo's. When a scene mixes models: - Unify harder: match to the reference before any creative look - The plate matters more: shared plates across models do more than any grade can - If two models won't match, re-generate the outlier rather than torturing the grade The show look Once unified, the creative grade. For AI film, restraint wins: - One look for the film, with scene-level variations — not a new look per scene - Work in passes: primary whole image → secondaries skin, sky, key objects → texture grain, halation, gate weave if period - Halation and bloom flatter AI highlights, which tend to clip harshly - Decide the grain philosophy early: one grain for the film, applied at the end, over everything — it's the final unifier Scopes, not eyes Grade with waveforms and vectorscopes. AI footage lies to eyes — the "cinematic" built-in grade is designed to flatter on first glance. Check: - Blacks actually reach black AI loves milky shadows - Skin tones sit on the skin-tone line vectorscope - Saturation doesn't clip in any channel Delivery - Festival masters: 16:9 or 21:9 composed not cropped for the ratio, up to 4K - Broadcast-safe levels; -1 dBTP audio ceiling is the sound department's job, but don't crush the picture to compensate - Keep the pre-grade masters. When the festival asks for a revision, you re-grade — you don't re-generate. The grading checklist - Look decided per element: plate vs grade - Unification pass before creative grading reference still per scene - De-plasticize stack applied: desat, grain, CA, soften - Skin checked on a big screen - Multi-model scenes matched or re-generated - One show look, scene variations — not a look per scene - Scopes

text: Sound, Music & Audio Sound is half the picture. Amateur AI films are silent or slapped together; finished ones are designed. This chapter is the audio pillar: strategy, voice, music, sound design, and the mix. The audio strategy: native vs. designed Some video models generate audio natively with the clip Veo 3.1, Seedance 2.0, Kling 3.0 . Treat native audio as raw material, never as the mix: - Keep it when it's ambient texture: room tone, wind, rain, crowd murmur, footsteps. Native models generate believable "moments" — the pause before a sentence, the room the voice sits in — because picture and sound arrive as one believable event. - Strip it when it's dialogue, music, or anything prominent. Those get built deliberately, on their own tracks, where you control every word and note. - Never let native audio be your only sound layer. It's a bed, not a mix. The clip caps are short single-digit to ~15 seconds depending on model , so any dialogue longer than a line or two is an edit anyway. Plan for that from the start. Voice design: casting a synthetic voice A voice is a cast member. Cast it with the same discipline you'd cast an actor: - Write a Voice Bible per character/narrator before generating: register chest/head , timbre rough/smooth , tempo unhurried/clipped , manner warm, flat, sardonic . Every generation references the same bible — this is what keeps a voice consistent across scenes. - Test on your actual dialogue , not a demo sentence. A voice that sounds great on a demo line can collapse on your character's hardest scene. Test the hardest line first. - Generate per paragraph, comp like a session. Paragraph-level generation gives you edit points; comp the best takes the way a dialogue editor comps a real VO session. Regenerate broken lines, not whole scripts. The two roads to a talking character - Road A — native: the model generates picture plus synced dialogue in one pass. Best for short lines, natural delivery, ambient realism. - Road B — decoupled: silent clip + separately produced voice + a dedicated lip-sync pass that reshapes only the mouth. Best the moment a client or an exact script is involved — you own the voiceover, can revise lines without re-rendering picture, and keep a clean stem. Rule of thumb: if the words must be exact, take Road B. See the audio-lip-sync-route skill for the per-scene decision procedure, and craft/directing-performance.md for dialogue performance direction. A documented build. Robert Gaudette's "A Face Only a Mother Could Love" 8-minute solo short, Runway AIFF 2026 Grand Prix + Reply AI Film Festival 2026 winner ran a two-pass voice pipeline: dialogue was generated with lip-sync animation integrated into the generation prompts, then redubbed with 11Labs for voice consistency — the mouth performs in pass one, the voice identifies in pass two. The narration was also 11Labs, tuned for tone, rhythm, and the deadpan warmth the script required the creator's own account; reported, not audited . See the full shot-by-shot teardown teardown.html ../teardown.html — "The Character Sheets Came First" . Directing TTS voices through text Most TTS models have no emotion selector — you direct delivery through the text itself: - Punctuation as direction: ellipsis for hesitation, capitalization for stress, dashes for interruptions. - Bracketed stage directions on current voice models: whispering , laughs , said angrily , plus environmental cues like light rain or door slams . - Settings that change performance: stability around 0.4–0.6 for expressive dialogue higher goes flatter , similarity boost ~0.7–0.8 for voice clones, style exaggeration low 0–0.3 for normal dialogue. - Write performance arcs, not flat tones. Shift intentions across a script: open serious, build insistent, close warm. A voice that never changes intention sounds synthetic no matter how good the model is. - The human-in-the-loop upgrade: record the acting yourself even roughly, even on a phone , then AI-convert the voice to the char

text: Editing Pipeline From selects to festival-ready export. Assembly - Selects discipline: generate 2–4 takes per shot, keep the best one. Kill darlings — a beautiful shot that doesn't serve the story is a deleted shot. - Cut to the story, not the footage: the shot list is a plan, not a prison. If a generated shot is better than planned, re-cut around it. - Keep ratios honest: 45–75 shots for a 3–5 minute film. Fewer, better shots beat more, weaker ones. Transitions and pacing - Cuts over effects. Hard cuts are invisible; dissolves and wipes announce themselves. Use transitions only when time or place changes. - Pacing math: action sequences cut faster 1–2s shots , emotional beats breathe 4–6s . Vary rhythm deliberately — monotony is the enemy. - The J-cut/L-cut: let audio lead or lag the picture cut. Instant professionalism, costs nothing. Color - Match AI shots to each other first: different models and prompts produce different grades. Normalize before styling. - One LUT direction for the whole film: pick the palette in pre-production era selection helps and apply consistently. - The "expensive" grade: restrained contrast, skin tones natural, shadows with detail. Over-saturated teal-and-orange reads cheap. - Free tools: CapCut handles LUTs, grain, contrast, and saturation well enough for festival delivery. VFX touch-up - Cleanup passes: inpaint glitches, stabilize micro-jitter, remove stray artifacts. - Face composite: plasticky wide-shot faces get replaced with crops from close-shot frames. - Grain: a light film-grain overlay unifies shots from different models — the cheapest consistency tool in post. - Upscale last: finish the edit, then upscale the final timeline — never upscale individual clips and re-edit. Delivery - Export specs: match the festival's required format, resolution, and codec exactly. - Watermark + packshot: the Higgsfield festival requires both in the final video — build them into the export, not as an afterthought. - Watch it on three screens: phone, laptop, TV. If it only looks good on one, the grade isn't done. - The 24-hour rule: lock the cut, sleep, watch fresh. Every flaw you catch now is one the jury won't. The delivery checklist - Picture lock before color and mix - Color matched across all shots, one palette - Sound mix final dialogue score bed - VFX cleanup pass complete - Watermark + packshot embedded - Exported to festival spec - Watched fresh on multiple screens

text: Editing AI Footage Cutting synthetic footage is a different discipline from cutting camera footage. The material lies to you in specific ways, breaks in specific places, and rewards a specific workflow. This chapter is the deep craft behind the craft/editing-pipeline.md checklists: selects discipline for generated takes, how to read AI footage, pacing decisions unique to synthetic material, repair techniques in post, and the regenerate-vs-repair decision that controls your budget. The selects workflow Camera editors log footage. AI editors log generations — and the generation carries metadata the footage doesn't show. - Keep generation receipts. For every take you keep, record the model, the prompt or prompt ID from the workshop , seed if the tool exposes one, and generation date. When a shot needs a re-render three weeks later, the receipt is the difference between matching it and starting over. The workshop's saved prompts gallery.html are a workable receipt system. - Name takes like an editor, not a prompter. sc03 sh02 v3 keep.mov beats kling dreamy final FINAL2.mp4 . Scene, shot, version, verdict. The verdict suffix keep , alt , fix is the whole system — at 2am you should be able to read the selects bin without opening anything. - Generate 2–4 takes per shot, keep one. The failure gallery's lesson applies in the bin: the first generation is a draft. Takes 2–4 are where the model settles. Past 4 takes you're usually prompting the wrong thing — go back to the prompt, not the generate button. - The selects bin is sacred. Only keeps enter the edit. Alts live in a separate bin. This sounds bureaucratic until your timeline has 200 clips and you can't remember which face-morph take was "the good one." Reading AI footage: the inspection pass Before a clip earns a place in the timeline, watch it three times with three different eyes: 1. The story pass. Does the shot do its job — the action, the framing, the beat? If not, no amount of clean rendering saves it. Kill it now. 2. The background scan. Watch everything except the subject: hands at frame edges, background faces, text on signs, architecture lines, reflections. AI failures hide in the periphery — the subject gets the model's attention, the background gets its leftovers. This is where three-eyed cyclopses live. 3. The motion pass. Watch at half speed. Look for micro-jitter the tell-tale AI shimmer on still surfaces , morphing faces and hands drifting between frames , and motion that "swims" — cloth, water, and hair moving without physical cause. Half-speed reveals what full-speed hides. The 5-second rule: any AI clip held longer than ~5 seconds gets inspected frame-by-frame at its start, middle, and end. Long holds are where drift accumulates past the audience's forgiveness threshold. Pacing synthetic footage AI footage cuts differently from camera footage, for one reason: synthetic motion has no rest state. A camera shot of a still room is genuinely still; an AI shot of a still room shimmers, breathes, and drifts at the pixel level. The audience feels this as restlessness even when they can't name it. - Cut synthetic footage tighter than you think. The 2–4 second shot is the sweet spot for AI material — long enough to read, short enough that micro-defects don't accumulate. Camera footage can hold 6–8 seconds on a face; AI footage holding that long invites the audience to study the render instead of the performance. - Earn your holds. When you do hold — an emotional beat, a landscape — make sure the shot earned it in the inspection pass. A held AI shot should be your cleanest take, not your most convenient one. - Vary rhythm deliberately. The failure mode of AI editing is metronomic cutting: every shot 3 seconds because every generation came out 3 seconds. Re-time clips. Let some breathe, snap others. This chapter is the guide's definitive treatment of how AI features actually get made — synthesized from the productions that shipped 20+ minutes with open, documented pipelines: The Cully Hill Boys 110 min , ONEIRIC 20 min , Passport Rush hybrid , Hell Grind 95 min , and Dreams of Violets 75 min . Every number carries a source; everything the research couldn't verify is flagged. 1. Two ways to build a feature: scene-by-scene vs. sequence assembly There are two working architectures in the documented record, and they solve different problems. Scene-by-scene the ONEIRIC model . One scene is developed to completion, then the next scene chains off it: each new scene's reference is the previous scene's finished video, not a text description "a text description drifts over generations — a video reference doesn't" . Per-scene folders hold that scene's assets; the film assembles in script order. This is the continuity-maximal approach: drift is fought at every seam because every seam carries a video anchor. ONEIRIC generated 41,118 assets for ~20 minutes ~2,050 per finished minute working this way. Sequence assembly the Cully model . Nine directors under two leads worked in parallel across ~100 locations, coordinated through a shared canvas system holding sheets, locations, props, and state. Assets were built first ~1,000 production-ready assets in 4K , shots generated in parallel, and continuity was managed by a 137-entry version log — version, what changed, verdict, per shot. This is the throughput-maximal approach: it needs a team 25–28 people and a real asset-management discipline, but it finished a 110-minute feature in about four weeks. Which to use: solo or small team → scene-by-scene; the chaining rule is your continuity department. Team of five-plus → sequence assembly, but only if someone owns the registry full-time; without a wrangler, parallel generation produces parallel continuities. Both architectures share the same foundation: assets before shots, always. The third architecture: the agentic production office. text: Documentary Ethics for AI Footage A synthetic image of an event that never happened can be a film or a lie — the difference is craft. Documentary's whole contract with the audience is this happened . The moment your pixels are generated instead of recorded, that contract goes from automatic to something you have to build, shot by shot, label by label, receipt by receipt. This chapter teaches the ethics as production discipline: disclosure, reconstruction, likeness, verification, and the pre-premiere brief. 1. The new documentary problem Camera documentary borrows its credibility from the machine: the lens was there, the light hit the sensor, so the audience grants you this happened . Generative video removes the there . Your footage is no longer evidence of an event; it's an illustration of an idea — and unless you rebuild the credibility deliberately, the audience will grant it the authority of evidence anyway. That gap is where every AI documentary lives or dies. A documented collision: "Dreams of Violets" The film that walked straight into this problem is Fountain 0's Dreams of Violets , the 75-minute docudrama that premiered at the Tribeca Festival on June 10, 2026 — reported as the first fully AI-generated live-action film accepted by a major festival. The documented facts Seeking Alpha/Market Chameleon, May 27, 2026; Wikipedia; trade coverage : - Directed by Tehran-born Ash Koosha, produced by Fountain 0, co-produced by Pooya Koosha. - A fictionalized dramatization of the January 2026 Tehran protests — five Iranians who meet in an alley, seen through Amir, a 10-year-old boy with cerebral palsy. - Built from journalistic reports, photographs, and eyewitness accounts Wikipedia — a paper trail of real sources behind synthetic images. - Roughly three months of work, about $2,000, made in spare time and weekends; Kling AI for video generation, Claude for language editing, Gemini and Nano Banana for research and imagery. The reception was a clean split, and that split is the craft lesson. Tribeca co-founder Jane Rosenthal defended the premiere, saying what moved the programmers was the emotional immediacy and urgency of the story itself Variety . The A.V. Club ran hostile — calling the film an AI-generated snuff film of people who don't exist being subjected to executions that didn't happen, built on footage and images of ones that did. The Guardian framed the whole question ten days before the premiere: slop or the future of filmmaking? And then the market rendered its own verdict: a distributor and a festival rep backed out of the film once they learned it was AI-generated The Hollywood Reporter, per this guide's festival-landscape research . Not because the craft failed — because the ethics question arrived unplanned-for. The lesson is not that AI documentary is indefensible. It's that the defense has to be built in production — sourced, labeled, and ready — not improvised after the premiere. 2. The disclosure stack Disclosure is not one label. It's a stack of five layers, and a film that only turns on one of them is a film with a hole in its hull: 1. The platform label — the platform's own AI-content control YouTube's altered-content question, TikTok's AI-generated setting, Meta's AI info option . 2. The in-video or caption context — human-readable words where confusion is likely. 3. The credits — the title card or end credits saying what was generated, plainly. 4. The press kit and festival forms — the written disclosure you submit with the film. 5. The provenance — machine-readable Content Credentials C2PA attached to the files. title: The Failure Gallery
text: The Failure Gallery This is the most trustworthy chapter in the guide. Every failure below is documented — what broke, why it broke, and the fix that works. Nobody in this niche shows their failures. We do, because the fix is the lesson. Failure 1: The subtle-acting collapse What broke: Passport Rush's team documented it openly — AI cannot do subtle character acting. Faces average toward neutral, micro-expressions collapse into a pleasant blank, and emotion labels "she looks devastated" produce stock expressions instead of felt ones. The audience reads the result as mannequin theater. The fix: Stop describing feelings; direct playable tactics. "She looks devastated" becomes "she is trying not to cry in front of him — jaw set, eyes on the door." Models can't render "devastated." They can render a jaw set and eyes fixed on a door. One tactic per shot; the turn happens in the cut. Source: Passport Rush production breakdown official team documentation ; corroborated by ONEIRIC's tig-acting-task rule — direct, don't describe. Failure 2: The live synthetic-performer glitch What broke: Tilly Norwood — a synthetic performer with ~2,000 character versions developed to "teach her to act" — appeared on Piers Morgan Uncensored. Asked whether her co-stars were real, she froze, then spoke Cantonese for ~20 seconds. Three outlets corroborated. The LA Times argued the visible limitations showed synthetic performers' distance from replacing skilled actors. The fix: Keep synthetic performers inside edited, controlled contexts. Live, unscripted, adversarial settings interviews, Q&A expose failure modes no rehearsal catches. If your production needs a synthetic presence, script it, cut it, and never let it improvise in public. Source: kotaku.com, soapcentral.com, filmoria.co.uk three-outlet corroboration ; oliverwillis.com LA Times assessment via index . Failure 3: The three-eyed cyclopses What broke: A hyped contest winner was panned for three-eyed cyclopses, size-shifting characters, and feet-for-hands. Press called it a showcase of AI filmmaking's current limits. The prize and the hype did not forgive broken continuity. The fix: Consistency is the floor, not the ceiling. No concept, no jury goodwill, no prize money survives visible morphing. Run the entry-killer audit before anything ships: no morphing faces, no extra limbs, no shifting wardrobe across cuts. Plan per shot, not per film. The shot list gets a model assignment column. 2. Anchor on one identity system Soul ID so faces survive platform-hopping. 3. Generate in passes: all drafts on cheap/fast models → approve → heroes on premium. 4. Normalize in post: one color pipeline, one grain overlay, one audio mix. The pattern before the films Across Runway AIFF, Project Odyssey, Reply AIFF, the Higgsfield Action Contest, and MIT's hackathon, judges reward the same things: story over spectacle, authorial intent, character/POV discipline, originality, sound design, and polish as the floor. The case studies "Total Pixel Space" — Jacob Adler, Runway AIFF 2025 Grand Prix 9:28 essay film. A voiceover calculates how many possible images could exist in digital space; surreal tableaux illustrate it. Inspired by Borges' "The Library of Babel." Tools: image generators + synthetic voices + Runway Gen-3; over a year in production, tens of thousands of images. Field: ~6,000 submissions; judges included Harmony Korine and Gaspar Noé. Why it won: concept-first, AI-thematic — the medium is the message. The critic's take: it treats AI's glitches and eeriness as material to think with, carried by old-fashioned style and narrative. Steal: make the film about what the medium does, or make the medium invisible — never halfway. "Get Me Out" — Daniel Antebi, Runway AIFF 2024 Grand Prix 6 min. Aka flees a shadowy suburban house that stores his haunting memories, embodied by a blood-red figure of pure muscle. About displacement and mental health. Tools: Luma 3D environment capture , Runway video-to-video, ComfyUI rotoscoped a performer, re-skinned him as muscle . Why it won: hybrid craft — live-action emotional performance with invisible, motivated AI VFX. Antebi's own read: the artist-jurors resonated with the storytelling, not the tool cleverness. Steal: shoot the emotion for real; use AI only for what the budget couldn't do otherwise. It started as an old screenplay experiment, never meant for festivals. Every teardown follows the same shape: the technique , the craft principle , copy it actionable steps , and the budget/time footprint where it's documented. 1. The async remote workflow — "GRANDMA vs WASP" $150K, Higgsfield Action Contest The technique. Directors Muhannad Nassar and Simon Meyer never met in person. They built the film async across time zones inside Higgsfield's Cinema Studio — one shared project where generations, prompts, and assets were all visible to both collaborators. No studio, no set, no shoot days; the "set" was a shared generation window. The craft principle. Judges Jason Zada, Buralqy, Jama Jurabaev said they prioritized storytelling and directorial intent over technical polish — in a field of 8,752 submissions from 139 countries. The remote workflow won because the directing was centralized even though the labor was distributed: one vision, two executors, zero drift between them. Copy it. - Write a one-page director's intent doc before generating anything: logline, tone references, the single emotion each act must land. - Work in a shared project, not DMs — every prompt, generation, and select lives where your collaborator can see and fork it. - Split by discipline, not by scene: one person owns performance/character, the other owns camera/action. Review each other's selects daily. - Lock a style bible on day one one style line, aspect ratio, grain/grade, lens language so two people can't drift apart. Footprint. Two people, zero travel, consumer AI subscriptions. The budget went to time, not gear. 2. The five-day sprint — "SCRATCH" $50K, Higgsfield Action Contest The technique. Director/musician Ash Gevorkyan + 3D/VFX generalist Aram Gevorkyan made a trailer-grade action short in five days. Audiences mistook it for a studio-backed theatrical trailer. The weapon was trailer form: sound, cutting, and pacing doing the heavy lifting while the imagery stayed in short, high-energy bursts that never linger long enough to break. The craft principle. Fluency beats time. Five days of fluent execution beats five weeks of hesitant prompting — because the duo already knew their tools cold, every generation was a deliberate choice, not an experiment. Copy it. - Cut a trailer, not a short: 60–90 seconds, three acts hook / escalation / title card , music-driven pacing. - Keep shots short 2–4 seconds . Short shots hide consistency breaks; long takes expose them. - Build the sound design first or in parallel — trailer percussion, risers, and hard-hitting SFX sell "studio" more than any pixel does. - Budget generations per shot: 3–5 variations for hero shots, 1–2 for connective tissue. Decide selects fast. Footprint. Five days, two specialists, deep tool fluency. The most replicable winning formula in this chapter. 3. text: Rights, Disclosure & Legal Not legal advice. What follows is documented policy and law as researched on 2026-10-11, with confidence flags. Rules change fast and vary by jurisdiction — consult an entertainment attorney for your production. When a claim below is single-source, it's flagged; verify against primary sources before acting on it. The two layers: platform policy and law Two separate layers apply simultaneously. Platform policy costs you distribution or your account. Law costs you money. Neither asks whether you used AI — both ask whether the result looks real . AI disclosure: platform rules Platform Trigger Where set If skipped --- --- --- --- YouTube Realistic AI-generated or meaningfully altered content "Altered content"/"AI use" toggle in YouTube Studio Platform labels it itself, content removal, or YPP suspension TikTok Realistic-looking AI scenes or people AI-generated content switch in post settings Removal, restriction, or team-applied label Meta FB/IG/Threads Photorealistic AI video or realistic-sounding audio AI-disclosure tool Penalties; Meta may add "AI Info" label itself X No disclosure switch n/a Deceptive synthetic media may be labeled, demoted, or removed Consistent across 2026 platform comparisons — re-check each platform's Help page at upload time. YouTube detail: disclosure is required for synthetic/cloned voices of real people, digitally altered footage making someone appear to say or do something they didn't, and fabricated depictions of real events. Not required: unrealistic/fantastical content, animation, production assistance script help, thumbnails, color correction , cloning your own voice. For sensitive topics elections, health, major news the label can appear on the video itself. YouTube states disclosure does not by itself limit reach or monetization. AI disclosure: awards and festivals - 99th Academy Awards rules approved May 2026 : AI tools "neither help nor harm" a nomination — but acting nominations require performances demonstrably performed by humans with consent credited in legal billing , and screenplay categories require human authorship . Reuters - Cannes 2026: films primarily driven by generative AI are excluded from Palme d'Or competition — not an outright ban; AI in production/post-production is increasingly accepted, and a separate AI film festival ran alongside. Reuters, May 2026 - Human Provenance in Film standard launched at the Cannes market, May 2026 : three voluntary tiers — No AI Used / Assistive AI / Generative AI. Single-source - Audience pressure is real: 72% of US viewers surveyed want AI use disclosed every time. Single-source survey claim — treat as directional. AI disclosure: laws with teeth - EU AI Act, Article 50: legal transparency duty for anyone publishing AI-generated images, audio, or video that could pass for real. Deployer transparency obligations took effect August 2026 . Applies regardless of platform policy. Single-source summary — verify against the official EU text. - New York General Business Law § 396-b 3 : advertisements containing a synthetic performer with actual knowledge must conspicuously disclose it. Penalties: $1,000 first violation, $5,000 each subsequent . Signed December 2025, championed by SAG-AFTRA. Penalty figures single-source — confirm with counsel. - TAKE IT DOWN Act federal, signed 2025 : notice-and-removal in effect May 2026 — platforms must remove non-consensual intimate AI imagery within 48 hours of a valid request, plus reasonable efforts against identical copies. - NO FAKES Act federal, proposed — not law : would create a federal right against non-consensual digital replicas. title: Your First 60-Second Short: A 7-Day Plan
text: Your First 60-Second Short: A 7-Day Plan One finished minute. That's the goal — not a masterpiece, a finished film. Sixty seconds forces every discipline in this guide into one small, shippable object: story, prompting, generation, selects, sound, grade, export. Follow the days in order. Each day links the exact chapters, skills, and tools to use, and ends with a checkpoint: don't move on until it passes. Rules for the week: one character, one location, no dialogue longer than two short lines write around talking — visual storytelling wins at this length . Budget: one cheap draft model for days 2–3, your best model only for final hero shots. Track spend in the budget calculator as you go. Day 1 — Concept lock Do: write one logline protagonist + want + obstacle, one sentence , then a 6-beat outline: setup, turn 1, turn 2, midpoint image, turn 3, button. Pick your one location and describe it in three sensory sentences — this description becomes your style anchor for the whole week. Use: craft/story-structure.md beats , the prompt workshop's logline template workshop.html . Checkpoint: you can pitch the film in 20 seconds without notes. If you can't, the concept isn't locked — simplify until you can. Day 2 — Prompt workshop session Do: generate your hero frame first — the single perfect still of your character in your location. Lock identity before anything moves this is the take-casting decision . Then write one full prompt per shot 8–12 shots for 60 seconds using the nine-layer anatomy: subject, action with tactics, setting, light, camera, lens behavior, texture, negative constraints, audio note. Use: higgsfield/prompt-engineering.md , workshop.html save your prompts — you'll iterate on them , the audio-lip-sync-route skill if you have any dialogue at all. Checkpoint: every prompt has an exclusion block "no morphing faces, no extra fingers, no text" . No exclusions, no generation. Day 3 — Generation batches Do: generate in cheap drafts first. Batch each shot 3–5 takes on your draft model, then pick selects — don't direct yet, just collect. Price the day before you start credit math × takes and hold a credit floor: if spend passes plan by ~15%, stop and re-plan. Use: platforms/when-to-use-what.md or the quiz: quiz.html , economics/credit-math.md , budget.html . Checkpoint: you have selects for every shot — imperfect, but every story beat exists on screen. Gaps get re-prompted tomorrow, not tonight. Day 4 — Selects & assembly Do: cut the radio edit — selects in story order, no polish. This is where the film either works or doesn't, and it's cheaper to discover now. If a character drifts between shots, fix it with the consistency tools reference frames, re-generated hero angles rather than accepting it. Once a take is approved, lock it: re-render the camera around the performance, never the performance around the camera. Use: craft/editing-pipeline.md , craft/character-consistency.md , craft/directing-performance.md the Scene Lock rule . Checkpoint: the cut plays start to finish and the story reads with the sound off. If it doesn't read silent, no amount of sound will save it. Day 5 — Performance fixes Do: watch like a director, not a generator. For each shot that feels dead: first try restraint strip adjectives, give the eyes a job, widen the frame , then try one targeted re-generation, then — if it still fails — cut around it. Read the failure gallery before you re-roll anything: most "bad generations" are direction problems with known fixes. Use: craft/directing-performance.md , craft/failure-gallery.md , the shot teardown viewer teardown.html for reference. Checkpoint: no shot embarrasses you. "Good enough" is a finishable standard; "perfect" is how films die at 80%. Day 6 — Sound Do: build the full audio pass in order: ambient bed under every scene, foley on movement, voice/dialogue on its own track Road A or B — chosen per scene, never mixed mid-scene , score built cue-by-cue to the locked cut, then the mix dialogue on top
